entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Thomas the Slav, a formidable 9th-century Byzantine military commander of Slavic origin, rose to prominence through his service to the Empire before launching one of the most devastating civil wars in Byzantine history. His rebellion, spanning 821–823 CE, threatened the very foundation of the nascent Amorian dynasty and the stability of the Byzantine state, particularly its control over Anatolia and the Balkans. Initially a trusted confidante of Emperor Leo V the Armenian, Thomas's ambition and the widespread discontent simmering within the Empire provided the fertile ground for his audacious challenge to Emperor Michael II.

The core of Thomas's revolt was a multi-ethnic coalition, attracting significant support from various groups, including Slavs, Armenians, Georgians, and even elements of the Muslim population in Anatolia, who saw an opportunity to destabilize Byzantium. Proclaiming himself Emperor in 821 CE, allegedly with the support of the Abbasid Caliphate, Thomas rapidly gained control over most of Byzantine Asia Minor. His forces then crossed into Europe, laying a protracted and brutal siege to the capital, Constantinople, for over a year (December 821 – October 822 CE). The siege, involving a massive fleet and land forces, tested the city's formidable defenses and the resolve of Michael II, who ultimately repelled the attacks with strategic acumen and crucial aid from the Bulgarian Khan Omurtag.
